VERDICT: REJECT

The claimed minimum $t-1$ cannot be right, and a small case shows it. Take $t=2$ and $n \ge 8$. The value $t-1 = 1$ would require a $2P_4$-saturated graph with $\rho(G)=1$. For a graph, $\rho(G)=1$ holds only when $G$ is a matching plus isolated vertices. Such a graph is not $2P_4$-saturated for $n\ge 8$:

- If $G$ has two isolated vertices $u,v$, adding $uv$ gives a $K_2$ component, which creates no $P_4$ and so does not create a $2P_4$.
- If $G$ has two matching edges $ab$ and $cd$, adding $bc$ creates one $P_4$ ($a\text{-}b\text{-}c\text{-}d$). The graph $G+bc$ still contains no second vertex-disjoint $P_4$, because all other components are $K_2$'s or isolated vertices. So the new edge does not create a $2P_4$.

Hence no $2P_4$-saturated graph has spectral radius $1$, so $1$ is not the minimum. The proposed argument also has no real support: the "core" and "equitable partition" steps are asserted without computation, and the lower bound $\rho(G)\ge t-1$ is not justified. The true minimum should depend on $n$ and be strictly greater than $t-1$. For example, the join $K_{2t-1}\vee \overline{K}_{n-2t+1}$ is $tP_4$-free and appears saturated, but its spectral radius grows with $n$.

I am fairly confident in this verdict because the $t=2$ counterexample is concrete, though I did not verify the exact general answer.

CONFIDENCE: 4
